```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_plotly <- requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("htmlwidgets", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_plotly)
```

The static FHLUS plot shows the overall shape of the distribution. The
interactive plots let you go a step further and ask *which* neighborhoods drive
that shape. Hover over any part of the curve to see the geography it belongs to,
its values, and any other variables you're interested in.

This vignette covers:

1. how each geography appears on the curve,
2. interactive plots for a single result and for a policy comparison,
3. what the pop-ups show, and how to add your own variables,
4. saving plots as standalone HTML files, and
5. the underlying data and use in Shiny.

The interactive functions need two optional packages:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("plotly", "htmlwidgets"))
```

## Example data

We'll use 15 made-up census tracts. Each has a `GEOID`, housing units
(all and affordable), median income (the opportunity indicator), land area,
and two variables that aren't part of the FHLUS calculation: median rent and
poverty rate.

```{r data}

 library(fhlus)

set.seed(2024)
n <- 15
tracts <- data.frame(
  GEOID            = sprintf("06037%06d", seq_len(n) * 100),
  housing_units    = sample(80:900, n),
  affordable_units = sample(0:120, n),
  median_income    = round(runif(n, 35000, 150000), -2),
  land_area        = round(runif(n, 0.4, 3.5), 2),
  median_rent      = sample(1100:3400, n),
  pct_poverty      = round(runif(n, 0.03, 0.35), 3)
)
head(tracts)
```

## How each geography appears on the curve

`fhlus_score()` sorts the geographies from lowest to highest opportunity and
plots their cumulative shares. **Each geography is one segment of the curve:**

- the segment's **width** is the geography's share of the denominator (here,
  land area), and
- its **rise** is the geography's share of the numerator (here, housing units).

The slope of a segment is therefore the geography's **concentration**: its share
of units divided by its share of land. A concentration of 1.00× is exactly
proportional. 2.00× means the tract holds twice the units its land area would
imply, and 0.50× means half. Steep segments on the right (high opportunity)
raise the FHLUS score; steep segments on the left lower it.

## A single result

```{r single}
result <- fhlus_score(
  tracts,
  numerator   = "housing_units",
  rank_var    = "median_income",
  denom       = "land_area",
  missing_pct = 0.10,
  graph       = FALSE
)

fhlus_interactive(
  result,
  tooltip_vars  = c("Median rent" = "median_rent", "Poverty rate" = "pct_poverty"),
  show_ci_bands = TRUE
)
```

Hover over the red curve. The tract under the cursor is highlighted, its slice
of the x-axis is shaded, and a pop-up shows:

| Section | Contents |
|---|---|
| Header | The geography ID and its rank (1 = lowest opportunity) |
| Values | Median income; housing units and land area, each with its share of the total; concentration |
| Cumulative | Where the segment starts and ends on each axis, plus the CI range for the cumulative units |
| Extra variables | Median rent and poverty rate |

### Choosing the ID

By default, `fhlus_interactive()` uses a column named `GEOID`, `geoid`,
`GEOID20` or `GEOID10` if one exists. Otherwise it uses each geography's rank.
To use a different identifier, such as a neighborhood name, set `id`:

```{r id, eval = FALSE}
fhlus_interactive(result, id = "neighborhood_name")
```

IDs should be unique; you'll get a warning if they aren't.

### Adding other variables

`tooltip_vars` accepts **any column of the data you passed to `fhlus_score()`**,
whether or not it was used in the calculation. Named elements set the display
label; unnamed elements use the column name:

```{r tooltip-vars, eval = FALSE}
fhlus_interactive(result, tooltip_vars = c("Median rent" = "median_rent", "pct_poverty"))
```

### Other options

The interactive plot mirrors the static one, and takes many of the same
arguments:

- `show_ci_bands`, `ci_alpha`: CI ribbon (needs `missing` or `missing_pct`)
- `title`, `subtitle`
- `color_var`, `color_denom`: line colors (red and blue by default)
- `boundary_label`: legend label for the boundary points; `NULL` hides them
- `annotation`, `annotation_x`, `annotation_y`: the "FHLUS = X" label
- `highlight = FALSE` turns off the hover highlight
- `width`, `height`: size in pixels

## Comparing two policies

`fhlus_compare_interactive()` is the interactive counterpart to
`fhlus_compare()`. Here we compare all housing with affordable housing:

```{r compare}
result_aff <- fhlus_score(
  tracts,
  numerator = "affordable_units",
  rank_var  = "median_income",
  denom     = "land_area",
  graph     = FALSE
)

fhlus_compare_interactive(
  result, result_aff,
  label_a      = "All housing",
  label_b      = "Affordable",
  tooltip_vars = c("Median rent" = "median_rent", "Poverty rate" = "pct_poverty")
)
```

Hovering shows **one pop-up per tract**:

- **Shared details, shown once:** ID, rank, median income, land area, and the
  extra variables.
- **A block for each policy:** its unit count and share of the total, its
  concentration, and where its curve segment starts and ends.
- **Difference (A − B):**
  - *Share of total*: how many percentage points more of policy A's units are
    in this tract.
  - *Concentration*: the difference in concentration.
  - *Cumulative gap*: the vertical distance between the two curves at the end
    of this tract.

The tract is highlighted on both curves.

When the two results use the same geographies and denominator, as here, the
curves line up and there is a single hover target. If they don't (for example,
different denominators), each curve gets its own hover target, and the pop-up
is for the geography on whichever curve is closest. A geography that appears in
only one result is marked *Not in this result*.

## Saving as HTML

Any interactive plot can be saved as an HTML file that opens in any web browser,
without R:

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
w <- fhlus_interactive(result, tooltip_vars = c("Median rent" = "median_rent"))
fhlus_save_html(w, "fhlus_tracts.html")

# Or straight from a result; extra arguments go to fhlus_interactive()
fhlus_save_html(result, "fhlus_tracts.html", tooltip_vars = "median_rent")

# Comparisons: save the widget
cmp <- fhlus_compare_interactive(result, result_aff)
fhlus_save_html(cmp, "fhlus_comparison.html")
```

By default the file is **self-contained**: everything is embedded in that one
file (about 4 MB, mostly the plotly library), so you can email or post it as-is.
A single-file export needs pandoc, which comes with RStudio, Positron and
Quarto. Without pandoc, `fhlus_save_html()` warns you and puts the supporting
files in a `<name>_files/` folder next to the HTML. Keep that folder with the
file.

## The data behind the plot

`fhlus_segments()` returns the per-geography table that the plots are built
from:

```{r segments, eval = TRUE}
segs <- fhlus_segments(result, tooltip_vars = "median_rent")
segs
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `rank` | Geography ID and rank (1 = lowest opportunity) |
| `cum_denom_start`, `cum_denom_end` | Segment start/end on the x-axis |
| `cum_var_start`, `cum_var_end` | Segment start/end on the y-axis |
| `share_denom`, `share_var` | The geography's own share of the denominator/numerator |
| `concentration` | `share_var / share_denom`; `NA` if the denominator share is 0 |
| `cum_var_lowest`, `cum_var_highest` | Cumulative share under the two CI scenarios (only with `missing`/`missing_pct`) |
| raw columns | Rank variable(s), numerator, denominator, excluded area, tie breakers, `tooltip_vars` |

For example, to list the tracts most over- or under-represented relative to
their land area:

```{r top, eval = TRUE}
segs[order(-segs$concentration), c("id", "median_income", "housing_units", "concentration")]
```

Because the table is keyed by geography ID, it joins directly to spatial data
for mapping:

```{r join, eval = FALSE}
tracts_map <- dplyr::left_join(tracts_sf, segs, by = c("GEOID" = "id"))
```

## Using the plots in Shiny

The plots are ordinary plotly widgets, so they work with `plotly::plotlyOutput()`
and `plotly::renderPlotly()`. Every hover point carries the geography ID in
`customdata`, so the app can react to the hovered geography. This is the basis
for linking the curve to a map.

```{r shiny, eval = FALSE}
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  plotly::plotlyOutput("curve"),
  verbatimTextOutput("hovered")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$curve <- plotly::renderPlotly(
    fhlus_interactive(result, tooltip_vars = "median_rent", source = "fhlus")
  )
  output$hovered <- renderPrint({
    ev <- plotly::event_data("plotly_hover", source = "fhlus")
    if (is.null(ev)) "Hover over the curve" else ev$customdata
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

## Tips

- **Large inputs:** above 2,000 geographies, the plot automatically switches to
  WebGL rendering so hovering stays responsive.
- **Older results:** results from earlier fhlus versions don't record their
  column names. Pass `numerator`, `denom` and `rank_var` to
  `fhlus_interactive()` or `fhlus_segments()`.
- **`fhlus_compare()` objects** don't keep the underlying data. For an
  interactive comparison, pass the two `fhlus_score()` results to
  `fhlus_compare_interactive()`.
